Dear Senator Rafferty and Secretary Grant,

The Maine Association of School Nurses (MASN) Board of Directors is writing to express our professional concerns regarding the proposed language in An Act to Update Certain Duties Regarding Student Health Related to Communicable and infectious Disease. As the frontline healthcare providers in Maine's educational system, we believe the proposed changes may inadvertently compromise student safety and create procedural confusion within our schools.
Our concerns are centered on the following points:
1. Clinical Judgment vs. Symptom Observation The proposed language suggests that unlicensed,
non-medical school personnel would be responsible for identifying signs and symptoms of infectious
or communicable diseases. While non-medical staff can certainly observe and report basic symptoms, there is a significant difference between reading a list of symptoms and applying clinicaljudgment.

School nurses possess the specialized education, clinical expertise, and critical thinking skills required
to assess signs and symptoms of health problems and determine when a situation warrants escalation. 2. Clarity of Responsibility and Protocol The current proposal "muddies the water" regarding who is

ultimately responsible for the reporting of suspected infectious diseases. In the school setting, a clear
chain of command is vital for public health. It should remain the duty of the school nurse----or another
school-designated health pr0fessional--to evaluate the health of a student and notify the appropriate

members of school administration. 3. Alignment with Existing Guidelines Maine school districts already follow established, evidencebased protocols for reporting suspected or confirmed cases of communicable diseases. These
processes are developed in close alignment with the Maine CDC and the l\/laine Department of
Education. Introducing new, overlapping, or ambiguous language risks disrupting these existing

workflows and could lead to inconsistent reporting across districts.

I

4. The Referral Process and Student Safety When a student is suspected of having a communicable

disease, they should be referred to a medical professional, such as their Primary Care Physician (PCP)
or an Emergency Department, with the guidance and support of a school nurse. A school nurse acts as

the vital link between the school and the broader healthcare system; bypassing this clinical expertise in

the decision-making process may lead to unnecessary panic for families or, conversely, a failure to

identify serious public health risks.
While we understand the intent behind the proposed language, we strongly believe that school health
personnel must remain central to any decision-making process involving communicable diseases. We
urge the committee to reconsider the proposed language changes in this act to ensure the health and

safety of all lvlaine students.

Respectfully,
Janneke Strickland, on behalf of The Board of Directors Maine Association of School Nurses

Testimony of Laura Cyr, Ph.D., Federal and State Legislative Specialist, Maine Department of
Education
In Support of: L.D. 2046
An Act to Update Certain Duties Regarding Student Health Related to Communicable and
Infectious Disease
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
Sponsored by: Senator Rafferty
Date: February 5, 2026
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Education and Cultural Affairs:
My name is Dr. Laura Cyr; l am here today representing the Department speaking in support of
L.D. 2046, An Act to Update Certain Duties Regarding Student Health Related to Communicable and infectious Disease.
The overall purpose of this bill is to align Maine statute to the realities and current practices in
the field.
Section 1 updates �6301, the "Student Health" subchapter, and changes the title to "lnfectious Disease," which better defines the content of that section of statute. It updates and provides clarification around the responsibilities and duties of school personnel and the superintendent regarding infectious disease, specifically regarding student identification and notification. The statute, as currently written, is out of date with best practice.The newer language provides more general guidance on what constitutes a potential public health threat, such as communicable and infectious diseases. It also identifies a superintendent designee, should a superintendent be unable to respond at the time of an identified public health communicable or infectious disease threat. Furthermore, changing the language from "teachers" to "school personnel" is an
important detail -- all staff members at a school have an important role to play in protecting student health. In developing these changes to �6301, the Maine Department of Education (DOE) consulted with the Maine Center for Disease Control.
Section 2 makes a technical change regarding epinephrine use in schools. Specifically, it replaces the term "subinjector" in relation to epinephrine delivery devices to "automated device" to
reflectadvancements in available medical technology. "Subinjector" is related to subcutaneous injection in the subcutaneous muscle layers, whereas "automated device" is a broader term that can also include medical administration such as a nasal spray.
1

Sections 3 and 4 are simple clerical changes to statutory language to reflect the addition to �6401-B described in Section 5.
Section 5 updates statutes related to the duties of Maine DOE school nurse consultants and
school nurse liaisons. Currently, there is no requirement for these positions to provide guidance to the field.This change will reflecta vital component of the Maine DOE's work in amplifying best practices and providing technical assistance to the field.
Sections 6 and 7 amend �6403-A regarding school nurses. In Section 6, school nurse duties have
been revised to include reference to the Scope and Standards of Practicein School Nursing, along with the addition of applicable rules `adopted by the State Board of Nursing and laws under Title 32, Chapter 31. These items are the basis of guidance for school nursing in Maine. Section 7 clarifies that guidelines to the field on the provision of school health must be based on national and state standards and updated at least every 3 yea rs. These changes align with best practices
and requirements for school nurses, who must follow all laws, regulations, and best practices in
education and in the nursing field. The Department of Education is in support of L.D. 2046, An Act to Update Certain Duties
Regarding Student Health Related to Communicable and infectious Disease. I am happy to answer any questions the Committee may have, and l will be available for work sessions on this

Testimony of Maine Families for Vaccines in support of 2146 & 2071
Submitted by Caitlin Gilmet, Director
Good afternoon, members of the Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services Committee,
Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony on behalf of Maine Families for Vaccines in support of LD 2146 and LD 2071.
Maine Families for Vaccines was formed after the passage of Public Law 154, which protects kids
like my son, Thomas. Shortly after he started daycare as an infant, he caught chickenpox. Parents like me shared our stories, and Maine voters responded---- approving our strong school vaccine
law by a '73 percent majority. That vote reflected something simple and powerful: Maine families value vaccines and want systems that protect our kids.
Since then, our work has grown into a national network with 14 state--based Families for Vaccines chapters. Across states and across political lines, our polling and policy work show the same thing again and again: families want stable access to vaccines, clear rules, and systems they can
rely on without confusion or disruption. Pm proud that what started here in Maine has become a
model for grounding public health policy in science and the will of the people.
We do not take lightly that these bills ask Maine to step into a space that has traditionally been
anchored at the federal level. Under normal circumstances, states should be able to rely on consistent, science-driven federal guidance. Right now, with vaccines increasingly politicized, that stability can't be assumed. Federal advisory processes have become increasingly uncertain and, at times, out of step with the priorities of the pro--vaccine majority--especially in a state like Maine, where support for vaccination is strong and clear.
LD 2146 and LD 2071 are a practical response to that moment.
LD 2146 helps keep Maine's immunization system steady and predictable by preserving evidence--based standards and protecting against funding gaps if federal processes falter. lt's about continuity--making sure what works today keeps working tomorrow.
LD 2071 focuses on how families actually get care. Pharmacies are a routine part of health care for many Mainers, particularly in rural areas. This bill helps ensure vaccines remain available and
affordable in those settings, while keeping appropriate safeguards and oversight in place.
The impact of these choices is visible right now. States with lower immunization rates are experiencing serious measles outbreaks. South Carolina has reported more than 900 cases. Maine has reported just one, and public health officials expect limited spread because strong
protections are already in place.
That difference reflects policy decisions.

Maine has the opportunity to continue leading by reinforcing the systems that keep disease rates low and families protected. These bills are grounded in the approach Maine families already trust, with a focus on keeping those protections steady and dependable.
For these reasons, Maine Families for Vaccines urges the committee to support LD 2146 and LD
2071.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Caitlin Gilmet Portland
Maine Families for Vaccines

Testimony in Support of 2146 & 2071
Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson, and members of the Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services:
My name is Joseph Zamboni, and I submit this testimony in Support to 2146 81 2071 on
behalf of the Pro-Vaccine Legal Alliance (PVLA). PVLA is a project of American Families
for Vaccines (AFV), a growing national network of legal, public health, and medical experts dedicated to protecting access to safe, effective vaccines and supporting evidence--based immunization policy. Our work focuses on ensuring that laws and policies governing vaccination promote child health, equity, and public trust while remaining grounded in sound science and long--standing public health practice.
Taken together, these bills represent a thoughtful, evidence--based approach to strengthening Maine's vaccine infrastructure by expanding access, reducing inequities, and ensuring that vaccination policy remains grounded in scientific rigor, fiscal oversight, and professional accountability.
LD 2071 addresses barriers to vaccine access at the point of care. It expands pharmacist
authority in a limited and carefully structured manner, allowing pharmacists to prescribe, dispense, and administer certain FDA-licensed vaccines under clearly defined
circumstances. Pharmacists are among the most accessible healthcare professionals in
Maine, particularly in rural and underserved communities, and this bill builds on Maine's existing framework with appropriate guardrails.
Under LD 2071, pharmacists may independently prescribe influenza vaccines to
individuals age three and older and ACIP-recommended vaccines to adults. Administration of vaccines to minors outside influenza continues to require a valid prescription from a licensed prescriber, and any deviation from ACIP guidance requires an explicit medical-necessity determination by a licensed prescriber. This structure preserves physician oversight where clinically appropriate while reducing unnecessary barriers to routine vaccination. Similar scope--of-practice expansions have been upheld
in other states, and LD 2071 aligns with those precedents.

LD 2071 also addresses one of the most persistent barriers to vaccination, which is cost.
By requiring private insurers and MaineCare to cover vaccines without deductibles, copayments, or coinsurance, the bill aligns with well--established public-health evidence demonstrating that eliminating cost--sharing increases vaccine uptake and reduces preventable disease. The Legislature has broad authority to impose insurance coverage requirements in furtherance of public health, and Maine has exercised that authority in
other contexts without legal issue.
Some may raise concerns regarding the bill's treatment of off-label vaccine use. Federal law already permits off-label prescribing of FDA-approved drugs, including vaccines. LD
2071 does not authorize pharmacists to independently determine off--label use. Instead,
it conditions administration on a valid prescription and a medical-necessity determination by a licensed prescriber, consistent with existing standards of care. In other words, the bill does not expand off--label use; it ensures that medically appropriate, evidence--supported care is not denied due to insurance exclusions.
LD 2146 complements these access improvements by strengthening Maine's vaccine
delivery system at the policy and infrastructure level. It addresses three real--world challenges facing vaccine programs today: evolving public-health guidance, gaps in federal vaccine funding, and uncertainty around liability for frontline providers. The bill operates squarely within Maine's public-health authority and is consistent with federal vaccine law
First, LD 2146 clarifies the decision--making framework of the Maine Vaccine Board by
allowing the Board to consider recommendations from the Department of Health and
Human Services and regional public-health collaboratives, such as the Northeast Public
Health Collaborative. Importantly, the bill does not weaken or replace ACIP standards. It preserves ACIP as the baseline while allowing Maine to respond flexibly to emerging
epidemiological risks, vaccine supply disruptions, or new evidence that may develop
more rapidly than national schedules. This reflects the practical reality that evidence--based immunization practice can evolve faster than formal national guidance during periods of disruption or emerging threat.
Second, LD 2146 authorizes the Maine Vaccine Board to seek state funding, subject to legislative approval, when federal Vaccines for Children funds are insufficient to cover recommended vaccines for eligible children. Federal law establishes minimum standards for VFC eligibility and funding but does not prohibit states from supplementing those
programs. This provision ensures continuity and equity of access so that children do not lose access to recommended vaccines simply because federal funding lags behind
public-health need.

Third, the bill provides limited civil--liability immunity for licensed pharmacists who administer vaccines outside ACIP guidelines, but only when they meet licensure and
training requirements and act in accordance with state or regional public--health guidance. This is not blanket immunity. It preserves professional licensing oversight and does not shield gross negligence or misconduct. Similar liability protections exist in emergency response and other public--health statutes nationwide and are routinely
upheld when narrowly tailored to serve a legitimate public--health purpose.
Together, LD 2071 and LD 2146 form a cohesive and responsible approach to vaccine policy in Maine. They expand access where barriers exist, preserve scientific and clinical
standards, maintain legislative and fiscal oversight, and support the healthcare
professionals who deliver vaccines on the ground.
For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Committee to vote Ought to Pass on both LD 2071 and LD 2146.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Testimony of American Families for Vaccines
In Support of LD 2146 and LD 2071
Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony on behalf of American Families for Vaccines in support of LD 2146 and LD 2071.
American Families for Vaccines is a national organization that works with families, health professionals, and state-based partners to support evidence--based immunization policy and protect access to routine vaccines. Our focus is ensuring that vaccine policy remains grounded in science, functions reliably for families, and continues to deliver the public health benefits it was designed to achieve.
Maine is widely recognized as a leader in this space. In 2019, Maine voters sent a clear and decisive message in support of strong vaccine protections. Since then, other states
have looked to Maine as an example of how to maintain high immunization rates,
minimize preventable disease, and build public trust in public health policy.
At the national level, that stability has become harder to maintain. Federal advisory and funding processes that states have long relied on to anchor immunization programs have become increasingly unpredictable. While federal guidance remains important,
states now face a growing need to ensure continuity and clarity on their
own--particularly in states like Maine, where vaccine confidence is high and the public expects systems to function smoothly.
LD 2146 responds directly to that challenge. The bill helps ensure that Maine's immunization framework remains stable even during periods of federal uncertainty. It protects continuity in standards and funding so that vaccine access does not depend on shifting national dynamics. From a public health perspective, this kind of structural
resilience is critical to keeping routine vaccination routine.
LD 2071 addresses another essential component of system performance: delivery. Across the country, primary care capacity constraints have made pharmacies an increasingly
important part of routine vaccination. This bill recognizes that reality and helps ensure vaccines remain available and affordable through familiar, accessible settings, while maintaining appropriate safeguards and oversight. Clear rules around coverage and delivery reduce confusion for families and providers alike.

Taken together, these bills strengthen Maine's ability to sustain the outcomes it has already achieved. They reinforce the systems that keep immunization rates high and
prevent the re--emergence of serious, vaccine--preventab1e diseases.
Recent measles outbreaks in states with lower vaccination coverage underscore what is at stake. Maine's limited measles activity stands in contrast, reflecting years of deliberate policy choices that prioritize prevention and public health stability.
American Families for Vaccines supports LD 2146 and LD 2071 because they help ensure those protections endure. These bills align with best practices we see emerging across
states and reflect a proactive approach to maintaining effective immunization systems in a changing national environment.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Northe Saunders, President
American Families for Vaccines and American Families for Vaccines Action Fund
